citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$, write $X_n\Rightarrow X$, or
$X_n\to X$ **in distribution**, when
$$F_{X_n}(x)\longrightarrow F_X(x)$$
at every continuity point $x$ of $F_X$. Here $F_X$ is the CDF from
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]] and continuity
points are those of [[def-atom-and-continuity-point-of-a-law]].

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

Let $P$ be $\phi$-irreducible with nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$. It is **Harris recurrent relative to $\phi$** if for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every starting state $x$, the first hitting time $\tau_A=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in A\}$ satisfies $\Pr_x(\tau_A<\infty)=1$. This is an all-start almost-sure hitting property; it is stronger than $\phi$-irreducibility, which requires only positive probability at some finite time.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathsf X=\{0,1\}$, $P(0,\{0\})=P(1,\{1\})=1$, and let $\pi(\{0\})=\pi(\{1\})=1/2$. The identity kernel leaves $\pi$ invariant, so the chain initialized with $X_0\sim\pi$ is stationary by [F2]. Set $f(0)=-1$ and $f(1)=1$. Then $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)=1$.

The transition is deterministic, hence $X_k=X_0$ for every $k$ and $S_n:=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)=nf(X_0)$. Thus $S_n/\sqrt n=\sqrt n f(X_0)$ takes values $\pm\sqrt n$ with equal probabilities. For each fixed $t>0$, once $n>t^2$ its distribution function at $t$ is $1/2$, while any $N(0,\sigma^2)$ has distribution function strictly greater than $1/2$ at $t$ when $\sigma^2>0$ and equal to $1$ when $\sigma^2=0$. Since $t$ is a continuity point of every such normal law, [F4] rules out convergence to any normal distribution.

Choose $\phi=\pi$ and $A=\{1\}$. Then $\phi(A)=1/2>0$, but $P^n(0,A)=0$ for every $n\ge1$ because the chain stays at $0$. By [F5] the chain is not $\phi$-irreducible and is not Harris recurrent relative to $\phi$. This counterexample shows only that finite variance without an ergodicity assumption does not guarantee a root-$n$ CLT.

Let $\delta>0$ and let $(b_n)_{n\ge2}$ be positive integers. Say that the sequence satisfies the **Flegal–Jones OBM batch-size conditions for exponent $\delta$**, with the integer monotonicity correction described below, when $b_n<n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$, and there is a constant $c\ge1$ such that
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(b_n/n)^c<\infty,$$
while
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\log n\to0,\qquad \frac{n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3}{b_n}\to0,$$
there are $n_0\ge2$ and $c_1<\infty$ with $\log n/b_n\le c_1$ for all $n\ge n_0$, and
$$b_n^2n^{-2}\log\log n\to0,\qquad b_n^4n^{-3}\log\log n\to0.$$

These are all the numerical rate, summability and endpoint hypotheses of Flegal–Jones Theorem 2. The source additionally asks that both $b_n$ and $n/b_n$ be nondecreasing. Those two requirements are omitted here: for an integer sequence with $b_n<n$ eventually they are incompatible with $b_n\to\infty$. Indeed, ratio monotonicity would imply $n(b_{n+1}-b_n)\le b_n<n$, while integer monotonicity would force the nonnegative integer $b_{n+1}-b_n$ to be zero. Thus the literal source conditions would make $b_n$ eventually constant. The corrected interface preserves the intended floor-power batch sequences, and the Brownian quadratic-form proof of OBM consistency needs neither monotonicity assumption.

This is a sufficient-condition interface; failure of a condition does not imply inconsistency of the estimator.

For the floor-power sequence $b_n=\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$, the intended source range $\delta>2/3$ and $2/(2+\delta)<\nu<3/4$ satisfies this corrected contract. Indeed, eventually $n^\nu/2\le b_n\le n^\nu$. Choose $c>\max\{1,1/(1-\nu)\}$ to bound the summability series by $\sum_n n^{-c(1-\nu)}<\infty$. The other displayed quantities are bounded respectively by $n^{\nu-1}\log n$, $2n^{2/(2+\delta)-\nu}(\log n)^3$, $2n^{-\nu}\log n$, $n^{2\nu-2}\log\log n$ and $n^{4\nu-3}\log\log n$, all tending to zero. Also $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n<n$ eventually. These checks establish the numerical contract without asserting the impossible simultaneous monotonicity.

**Inputs:** Real outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, an integer $n\ge2$, and an integer batch size $b$ with $1\le b<n$. For an MCMC run, $y_i=f(X_i)$ for the chosen real-valued observable $f$.

**Outputs:** The sample mean $\bar y_n$, the overlapping-batch-means estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}$, and its estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

1. Compute the sample mean
$$\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.$$

2. For each starting index $j=1,\ldots,n-b+1$, compute the overlapping batch mean
$$\bar y_j(b)=\frac1b\sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}y_i.$$

3. Return the overlapping-batch-means variance estimate
$$\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}=\frac{nb}{(n-b)(n-b+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b+1}\bigl(\bar y_j(b)-\bar y_n\bigr)^2.$$

4. Return the estimated Monte Carlo standard error
$$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar y_n)=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}/n}.$$

All sums are finite, the denominator is positive because $b<n$, and the variance estimate is nonnegative. The procedure always returns a number for the stated finite input. It does not by itself assert a CLT or consistency; consistency requires the hypotheses of the overlapping-batch-means theorem.

derivations.claim: For $n\ge2$, $n^{1/2}-1<b_n\le n^{1/2}$, so $b_n/n^{1/2}\to1$. Thus $n^{2/3}(\log n)^3/b_n\sim n^{1/6}(\log n)^3\to\infty$, which violates the required limit in [F1] at $\delta=1$.
Since $1\le b_n\le n^{1/2}<n$ for $n\ge2$, the finite OBM procedure in [F2] is defined. Step 1.1 establishes failure of one source sufficient condition only, not inconsistency of the estimator.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ have a supplied countable algebra $\mathcal C$ generating $\mathcal X$, and let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$. If
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{for }\pi\text{-almost every }x,$$
then its stationary output process is strongly mixing:
$$\alpha_X(n)\longrightarrow0.$$

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, natural filtration $\mathcal F_k$, and ergodic canonical path shift. Let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Suppose there is a measurable $g\in L^2(\pi)$ such that $f=g-Pg$ $\pi$-almost everywhere, where $Pg(x)=\int g(y)P(x,dy)$. Put $D_{k+1}:=g(X_{k+1})-Pg(X_k)$ and $\tau_f^2:=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$. Then for every $n\ge1$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)=g(X_0)-g(X_n)+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D_{k+1},$$
and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\tau_f^2),$$
including the degenerate case $\tau_f^2=0$. If additionally $\sum_{k\ge1}|\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))|<\infty$, then
$$\tau_f^2=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k)),$$
so this CLT's variance equals the covariance long-run variance of [[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Let $S\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal E$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, and let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stochastic process with each
$Y_n:\Omega\to S$ a random element
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]). The process
$Y$ is **strictly stationary** when every finite-dimensional law is unchanged
by a common nonnegative time shift: for every $r\ge1$, every
$0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(Y_{m+n_1},\ldots,Y_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(Y_{n_1},\ldots,Y_{n_r}).$$

The **canonical path law** of $Y$ is the pushforward
$\mathbb P_Y=\mathcal L(Y)$ of $\mathbb P$ under the coordinate map
$\omega\mapsto(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$, a probability measure on the product
space $S^{\mathbb N_0}$ with its product sigma-algebra. The **left shift** is
$\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$ for $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}\in S^{\mathbb N_0}$.

A strictly stationary process is called **ergodic** when the canonical shift $\theta$ is ergodic
for $\mathbb P_Y$ in the sense of
[[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]. The shift-invariance needed for that
definition, namely that $\theta$ is measure preserving for $\mathbb P_Y$, is
proved below for strictly stationary $Y$, so in that case
$(S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0},\mathbb P_Y,\theta)$ is a
probability measure-preserving system in the sense of
[[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

derivations.claim: Put $v=v_\epsilon/(1-a^2)$. If $X_k\sim N(0,v)$ independently of $\epsilon_{k+1}$, then $aX_k+\epsilon_{k+1}$ is normal with mean zero and variance $a^2v+v_\epsilon=v$. Thus $\pi=N(0,v)$ is invariant, and initializing with $\pi$ gives a stationary chain by [F1].

Iterating the recursion gives $X_n=a^n x+\sum_{j=1}^n a^{n-j}\epsilon_j$ when $X_0=x$, so $P^n(x,\cdot)=N(a^nx,v_n)$ with $v_n=v(1-a^{2n})$. For each fixed $x$, $a^nx\to0$ and $v_n\to v$, so the Gaussian densities $p_n^x(y)$ converge pointwise to the density $p(y)$ of $N(0,v)$. For sufficiently large $n$, $v/2\le v_n\le v$ and $|a^nx|\le1$. On $|y|\le2$, $p_n^x(y)\le(\pi v)^{-1/2}$; on $|y|>2$, $|y-a^nx|\ge|y|/2$, hence $p_n^x(y)\le(\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-y^2/(8v)}$. This gives one integrable majorant for $p_n^x$; with $p$ added it also dominates $|p_n^x-p|$. By [F2], $\int|p_n^x-p|\,dy\to0$. Therefore $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\int|p_n^x-p|\,dy\to0$ for every $x$.
The Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R$ has the countable generating algebra of finite unions of rational half-open intervals and rational rays. Applying [F3] to step 1.2 gives $\alpha_X(n)\to0$.

Let $E$ be an event invariant under every power of the canonical left shift and put $p=\mathbb P(E)$. Finite-coordinate cylinders form a generating pi-system. The events approximable in probability by such cylinders form a sigma-algebra: complements preserve symmetric-difference probability, and for a countable union one first truncates by continuity from below and then approximates the finitely many sets. Hence for every $\eta>0$ there are $j$ and $A\in\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_j)$ with $\mathbb P(E\triangle A)<\eta$. For $m>j$, $B=\theta^{-m}E$ is measurable with respect to $\sigma(X_m,X_{m+1},\ldots)$, stationarity gives $\mathbb P(B)=p$, and shift invariance gives $E=B$. Thus $|p-p^2|=|\mathbb P(E\cap B)-p\mathbb P(B)|\le2\eta+\alpha_X(m-j)$. Let $m\to\infty$ using step 2.1 and then $\eta\downarrow0$; we obtain $p(1-p)=0$. By [F7], every invariant event having probability zero or one is precisely ergodicity of the canonical shift.

Set $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x/(1-a)$. Both are in $L^2(\pi)$ and $\pi(f)=0$. The kernel action is $Pg(x)=\mathbb E[(ax+\epsilon_1)/(1-a)]=ax/(1-a)$, so $g-Pg=f$. Also $D_{k+1}=(aX_k+\epsilon_{k+1})/(1-a)-aX_k/(1-a)=\epsilon_{k+1}/(1-a)$, whence $\mathbb E[D_{k+1}^2]=v_\epsilon/(1-a)^2$. Iterating the recursion gives $X_k=a^kX_0+\sum_{j=1}^ka^{k-j}\epsilon_j$. Independence implies $\gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_k)=va^k$. Since $|a|<1$, the covariance series is absolutely summable, and [F6] gives $\sigma_f^2=v+2v\sum_{k\ge1}a^k=v+2va/(1-a)=v_\epsilon/(1-a)^2$. This agrees with step 4.1, including $a=0$ and negative $a$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For a probability kernel $K$ on $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $I$ be the identity
kernel $I(x,A)=1_A(x)$ and define
$$ K^0:=I,\qquad K^{n+1}:=K^nK, $$ where composition is in chronological order: $$ K^{n+1}(x,A)=\int_E K(y,A)K^n(x,dy). $$
The identity map makes $I$ a probability kernel, including on a one-point
space. Induction using the published kernel-composition lemma shows that every
$K^n$ is a probability kernel. Associativity makes products of several copies
of $K$ unambiguous. No conditional-expectation version is selected and no form
of Choice is used.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f : X \to [0,+\infty]$ be measurable. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ define

$$s_k := \sum_{j=0}^{k2^k-1} j2^{-k}\, \mathbf{1}_{\{j2^{-k} \le f < (j+1)2^{-k}\}} + k\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge k\}}.$$

Then each $s_k$ is a simple measurable function,

$$0 \le s_k \le s_{k+1} \le f,$$

and $s_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x \in X$. If $E \subseteq X$ is a set on which
$f \le M < +\infty$, then $s_k \to f$ uniformly on $E$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal A_0$ be the algebra generated by $\{\{f<q\}:q\in\mathbb Q\}$. Inductively, let $\mathcal A_{j+1}$ be the algebra generated by $\mathcal A_j$ and all sets $\{x:P(x,A)>q\}$ with $A\in\mathcal A_j$ and $q\in\mathbb Q$. These are subsets in $\mathcal F$ by [F1] and [F6]. Each algebra is countable: enumerate its generators and then all finite Boolean expressions in them. This also explicitly enumerates $\mathcal A=\bigcup_{j\ge0}\mathcal A_j$. Put $\mathcal G=\sigma(\mathcal A)$. Since rational half-lines generate the real Borel sigma-field, $f$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable.

For $A\in\mathcal A$, all rational superlevel sets of $P(\cdot,A)$ belong to $\mathcal G$ by construction. The class $\mathcal D$ of $B\in\mathcal G$ for which $P(\cdot,B)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable contains $\mathcal A$ and $X$. It is closed under complements because $P(x,B^c)=1-P(x,B)$ and under countable disjoint unions because $P(x,\bigcup_lB_l)=\sum_lP(x,B_l)$ is a measurable increasing limit. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system, and [F2] gives $\mathcal D=\mathcal G$. The restriction $P_{\mathcal G}$ therefore is a probability kernel.

For every nonnegative $\mathcal G$-measurable $g$, integration against $P_{\mathcal G}(x,\cdot)$ agrees with integration against $P(x,\cdot)$: this holds for indicators by restriction, for nonnegative simple functions by finite additivity of the integral, and for general $g$ by [F7] and [F3]. Both integrals are allowed to be infinite. Induction in [F4], using this integration identity and step 1.2, gives $P_{\mathcal G}^n(x,B)=P^n(x,B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal G$, including $n=0$.

If $\pi$ is invariant, the same restriction identity for integrals gives $\int P_{\mathcal G}(x,B)(\pi|_{\mathcal G})(dx)=\int P(x,B)\pi(dx)=\pi(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal G$. This is invariance of $\pi|_{\mathcal G}$ by [F5]. All generating enumerations in step 1.1 were explicit, so this construction introduces no choice assumption.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] choose an orthogonal matrix $O$ with $A=O\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)O^T$. By [F2], $Z=O^TU$ has independent standard-normal coordinates. Integration by parts in the density [F3], with $ze^{-z^2/2}\to0$ at both infinities, gives $EZ_i^2=1$. Every absolute moment of $V_i=Z_i^2-1$ is finite: for an integer $k\ge1$, $|z^2-1|^k\le(1+z^2)^k$, and this polynomial is integrable against $e^{-z^2/2}$. Thus $EV_i=0$, $E(U^TAU)=\sum_i\lambda_i=\operatorname{tr}A$, and $U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_i\lambda_iV_i$.

Expand the even power $(\sum_i\lambda_iV_i)^{2r}$ over ordered tuples of $2r$ indices. By [F4], a term whose tuple has an index appearing exactly once has expectation zero. Group all other terms by the partition of their $2r$ positions into equal-index blocks. Such a partition has block sizes $k_1,\ldots,k_q\ge2$ with $\sum_a k_a=2r$. For each fixed partition, taking absolute values and dropping the restriction that different blocks have distinct indices bounds its contribution by $\prod_{a=1}^q E|V_1|^{k_a}\prod_{a=1}^q\sum_i|\lambda_i|^{k_a}$. All these quantities are finite by step 1.1.

Put $L=(\sum_i\lambda_i^2)^{1/2}$. If $L=0$, the centered form is identically zero and the bound holds. Otherwise $|\lambda_i|/L\le1$ and $\sum_i(|\lambda_i|/L)^2=1$, so for every integer $k\ge2$, $\sum_i|\lambda_i|^k\le L^k$. Consequently each partition contribution in step 1.2 is bounded by $L^{2r}\prod_a E|V_1|^{k_a}$. There are finitely many partitions of the fixed set of $2r$ positions; the sum of these moment products over the partitions without singleton blocks is a finite constant $C_r$ depending only on $r$.

Since $2r$ is even, the expanded power is the absolute $2r$th power. Summing the bounds of step 2.1 therefore gives $E|U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A|^{2r}\le C_r L^{2r}$. Finally $L^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=\sum_{i,k}A_{ik}^2$ by symmetry and orthogonal diagonalization. This proves the bound and the expectation assertion, including $A=0$, singular matrices and matrices of either sign.

$$P^m(x,A)\ge\epsilon\nu(A)\quad(x\in C,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
The inequality is pointwise in $x$ and holds for every measurable $A$.

A **geometric drift inequality outside $C$** consists of a finite-valued measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,\infty)$, constants $0<\lambda<1$ and $0\le b<\infty$, and
$$PV(x):=\int V(y)P(x,dy)\le\lambda V(x)+b\,1_C(x)\quad(x\in\mathsf X).$$
The terms small set and drift are separate hypotheses; neither definition asserts the existence of the other.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain, let
$\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ be a stopping time, and let $H$ be a
bounded measurable path functional. Put $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH$ and define the
everywhere meaningful random variables
$$ Z_H:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots), \qquad R_h:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}h(X_n). $$ Both are defined to be zero on $\{\tau=\infty\}$. Then $$ \mathbb E[Z_H\mid\mathcal F_\tau]=R_h\quad\text{a.s.} $$ This is the precise meaning of the usual eventwise notation $$ \mathbb E[1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}H(X_\tau,X_{\tau+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_\tau] =1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}h(X_\tau): $$
no value $X_\infty$ is used. If $\tau<\infty$ almost surely, the indicators can
be omitted.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let

and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
The sum of a complex power series is analytic on its open disc of convergence.
Every function analytic on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ is holomorphic on $U$.

If $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ has radius $R$, then for every $k\in\mathbb N$ and $|z-a|<R$,
$$f^{(k)}(z)=\sum_{n\ge k}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}c_n(z-a)^{n-k}.$$
Every derived series has radius $R$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Set $w_1(x)=\epsilon1_C(x)$ and $w_0(x)=1-w_1(x)$. On $\widetilde X=X	imes\{0,1\}$ define $K_{x,1}=
u$; define $K_{x,0}=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon
u)/(1-\epsilon)$ for $x\in C$, and $K_{x,0}=Q(x,\cdot)$ otherwise. The split kernel is
$$\widetilde Q((x,i),B	imes\{j\})=\int_B w_j(y)K_{x,i}(dy).$$

The same summation at each subsequent time shows that the $x$-coordinate path has the original $Q$-chain law. The set $\alpha=C	imes\{1\}$ is an atom: all its states have the identical outgoing transition obtained by using $
u$.

Put $\widetilde\pi(dx,i)=w_i(x)\pi(dx)$. Summing its incoming transitions first over $i$ gives $\pi Q=\pi$ and then assigns the new flag according to $w_j$, proving $\widetilde\pi\widetilde Q=\widetilde\pi$ by [F13]. Write $\mathbb P_\alpha=\mathbb P_\kappa$; its future after time zero is the same from every atom state. Starting in $\alpha$, the next coordinate law is $\nu$ and subsequent coordinate transitions are $Q$, so
$$u_0=1,\qquad u_n=\mathbb P_\alpha(Z_n\in\alpha)=\epsilon\nu Q^{n-1}(C)\quad(n\ge1).$$
The hypothesis implies $|u_n-p|\le c\theta^n$ for all $n\ge0$ after increasing a finite $c$.

$$U(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}u_nz^n=\frac1{1-F(z)},\qquad F(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}f_nz^n.$$

Near $z=1$ the expression
$$\widehat F(z)=1-\frac{1-z}{p+(1-z)J(z)}$$
is holomorphic and agrees with $F$ on its overlap with $|z|<1$. Indeed the denominator has value $p>0$ at $1$ and remains nonzero on a sufficiently small disk; the quotient is complex differentiable there by the difference-quotient formula for the derivative of a reciprocal. Letting $t\uparrow1$ and using [F7] and derivative continuity from [F11] gives $\sum_{n\ge k}f_n(n)_k=\widehat F^{(k)}(1)$. Choose a radius $\delta>0$ whose closed disk about $1$ lies strictly within this holomorphic neighborhood and a finite bound $B$ for $|\widehat F|$ on its circle. [F12] then bounds these nonnegative derivative values by $k!B\delta^{-k}$.

For $0<h<\delta$, the finite binomial expansion for each integer $n$, followed by [F8], yields
$$\mathbb E_\alpha[(1+h)^\tau]=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{h^k}{k!}\sum_{n\ge k}f_n(n)_k\le\frac{B}{1-h/\delta}<\infty.$$
Thus some $b>1$ has $\mathbb E_\alpha b^\tau<\infty$. The return is almost surely finite by step 2.1. This argument establishes an exponential moment from positivity and analytic continuation; it does not assume in advance that the original series $F$ converges beyond the unit disk.

Let $T=\inf\{n\ge0:Z_n\in\alpha\}$ and start the split chain from $\widetilde\pi$. By [F6], $I_j=1_\alpha(Z_j)$ have mean $p$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(I_0,I_n)=p(u_n-p)$. Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

derivations.claim: For a finite real $U$, write $T(t)=\mathbb P(|U|>t)$ for $t\ge0$. The tail tends to zero at infinity, is nonincreasing and is right-continuous. Thus $Q_U(u)$ is finite for $u>0$, is nonincreasing, and is Borel measurable. More precisely, $Q_U(u)>t$ if and only if $u<T(t)$: if $T(t)\le u$, then $t$ belongs to the set defining the infimum; if $T(t)>u$, right-continuity supplies an $\varepsilon>0$ with $T(t+\varepsilon)>u$, so that infimum exceeds $t$. Consequently Lebesgue measure on $(0,1)$ gives $\lambda\{u:Q_U(u)>t\}=T(t)$ for every $t\ge0$. The laws of $Q_U$ under $\lambda$ and of $|U|$ therefore agree on all closed left rays and both have total mass one. These rays form a pi-system and generate the Borel sigma-algebra: their differences give half-open intervals, and countable unions of those give all open intervals. By [F6] the laws agree, proving the stated integral identity. In particular $\int_0^1Q_U^2=\mathbb EU^2$.

Suppose first $U,V\ge0$ and $U,V\in L^2$. Their first moments and $\mathbb E(UV)$ are finite by [F3]. The threshold-indicator identities and [F5] give $\mathbb E(UV)=\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(U>s,V>t)\,ds\,dt$ and $\mathbb EU\mathbb EV=\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(U>s)\mathbb P(V>t)\,ds\,dt$. Both integrands have finite integrals, so their difference represents the covariance and the integral triangle inequality applies. The absolute threshold-indicator covariance is bounded by $a$, by $\mathbb P(U>s)$, and by $\mathbb P(V>t)$, since the joint probability and the product probability both lie between zero and either marginal probability.

Put $T_U(s)=\mathbb P(U>s)$ and $T_V(t)=\mathbb P(V>t)$. By [F5] and step 1.1,
$$\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\min\{a,T_U(s),T_V(t)\}\,ds\,dt=\int_0^a Q_U(u)Q_V(u)\,du.$$
Indeed the minimum is $\int_0^a\mathbf1_{\{u<T_U(s)\}}\mathbf1_{\{u<T_V(t)\}}\,du$, and each inner threshold set has length its quantile. The right-hand side is finite by Cauchy–Schwarz on $(0,1)$ and the squared-quantile identity in step 1.1; this particular integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality follows by integrating $(Q_U-cQ_V)^2\ge0$ and minimizing the resulting quadratic, with the zero-norm case immediate. Step 1.2 therefore proves the covariance bound with constant one for nonnegative $U,V$.

For real $U,V$, expand $\operatorname{Cov}(U^+-U^-,V^+-V^-)$ into four terms. Each nonnegative part has a tail quantile at most the corresponding absolute quantile, because its tail probabilities are smaller. The result of step 1.3 bounds each term by $\int_0^aQ_UQ_V$; the triangle inequality gives the asserted factor four. If $|U|\le A$ and $|V|\le B$, their absolute quantiles are bounded by $A,B$, so the bound becomes $4ABa$, including $a=0$ or either zero bound.

For complex $U,V$, expand $\mathbb E(UV)-\mathbb EU\mathbb EV$ into the four real bilinear covariance terms of their real and imaginary parts. Each real part is bounded in absolute value by $A$ or $B$, so step 2.1 and the complex triangle inequality give $16ABa$. Finally, for observations separated by $n$, both collection sigma-algebras are sub-sigma-algebras of the past and future fields appearing in [F1]; their event supremum is therefore at most $\alpha_Y(n)$. All assertions follow.

boundaries.evidence: The integral over [0,a] is zero for a=0; steps 1.3 and 2.1 give covariance zero, without an empty-domain quantile.
Step 2.1 includes A=0 or B=0; then the corresponding variable vanishes almost surely and both bounds are zero.
The probability space has mass one. Step 1.1 proves the quantile-law identity under unit Lebesgue measure on (0,1), and the event coefficient is bounded by one.
The law may be a point mass and either L2 norm may vanish; steps 1.1 and 1.3 explicitly include the zero-norm case.
Quantiles are defined on 0<u<1 only; step 1.1 treats t=0, zero tails, and arbitrary atoms by the exact generalized-inverse relation. Step 2.1 includes a=0.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{U,V}|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|,$$
where the last supremum is over real $U,V$ with finite second moments (square-integrable in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$, respectively, and each with positive variance. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1 \le p < \infty$. Then
every element of $L^p(\mu)$ can be approximated in $L^p$ by simple functions
whose supports have finite measure.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

derivations.claim: For finite $F\subset\mathbb Z$, choose an integer $m\ge0$ with $F+m\subset\mathbb N_0$ and prescribe the law of $(X_i)_{i\in F}$ to be that of $(Y_{i+m})_{i\in F}$. If $m'$ is another permissible shift, stationarity compares the smaller shift with the larger one, so the law is independent of the choice. Restrictions are consistent because finitely many coordinate sets can be translated by one common shift. Every coordinate space is the standard Borel space $\mathbb R$, so [F1] gives $Q$. Its nonnegative restriction equals the process law of $Y$ on cylinders and hence everywhere by [F5]. Translating finite sets does not change their prescribed laws, so $Q\circ T^{-1}=Q$ by the same uniqueness argument. Both $T$ and its inverse are measurable because their coordinate maps are coordinates.

For any subset $I\subset\mathbb Z$, let $\mathcal A_I$ be the algebra of events depending on finitely many coordinates in $I$. Every event in $\sigma(X_i:i\in I)$ can be approximated in symmetric-difference probability by $\mathcal A_I$. Indeed, the approximable events are closed under complements. For a countable union, first replace that union by a finite subunion with arbitrarily small lost probability, using continuity from below, then approximate its finitely many constituent events and apply the union bound. Thus the approximable events form a sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal A_I$. By [F4], approximate an $L^2$ variable by simple functions, and approximate the finitely many indicator events of each simple function by $\mathcal A_I$ events. For an indicator the squared $L^2$ error is its symmetric-difference probability; finite summation gives the required arbitrarily small $L^2$ error for a simple function. Consequently every such variable has finite-coordinate $L^2$ approximants.

First suppose $U$ and $V$ depend on finitely many coordinates in $(-\infty,k]$ and $[k+n,\infty)$, respectively. Translate all coordinates by one integer $m\ge0$ so that the used past coordinates and the split $k+m$ are nonnegative. Their joint distribution is an original-process distribution by step 1.1. The translated variables are measurable in $\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_{k+m})$ and $\sigma(Y_{k+m+n},Y_{k+m+n+1},\ldots)$, so [F2] proves the asserted covariance inequality when both variances are positive. A variable of variance zero equals its mean almost surely and has zero covariance, so the inequality holds then too. For arbitrary $U,V$, take step 1.2's finite-coordinate $L^2$ approximants. Their means, second moments, and covariances converge by [F3], so passage to the limit proves the same inequality.

Assume $\rho_Y(n)\to0$, and let $A$ satisfy $Q(A\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}A)=0$, with $p=Q(A)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, step 1.2 supplies a finite-coordinate event $C$ with $Q(A\mathbin\triangle C)<\varepsilon$; enlarge its coordinate support to $[-m,m]$ for some $m\ge0$. For $n>2m$, $C$ is in $\mathcal F_m$ and $T^{-n}C$ is in $\mathcal G_{n-m}$. Step 2.1 applied to their indicators gives $|Q(C\cap T^{-n}C)-Q(C)^2|\le\rho_Y(n-2m)/4$, since every indicator variance is at most $1/4$. Invariance modulo null sets and measure preservation imply $Q(A\cap T^{-n}A)=p$. The intersection changes in probability by at most $2\varepsilon$ upon replacing both copies of $A$ by copies of $C$, and $|p^2-Q(C)^2|\le2\varepsilon$. Hence $|p-p^2|\le4\varepsilon+\rho_Y(n-2m)/4$. Let $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ to obtain $p=p^2$. Therefore $p\in\{0,1\}$, proving [F6] and the stronger mod-null formulation claimed.

Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a real-valued
strictly stationary process with $\mathbb E|Y_0|<\infty$
([[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]), with canonical path law
$\mathbb P_Y$ and left shift $\theta$. Let
$\mathcal I=\{A:\theta^{-1}A=A\}$ be the strictly invariant sigma-algebra on
path space ([[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]). Then

$$\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Y_k\ \longrightarrow\ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P_Y}[z_0\mid\mathcal I]\circ\Phi \qquad\text{almost surely and in }L^1(\mathbb P),$$

where $\Phi(\omega)=(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$ and the conditional expectation is
that of [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. If moreover the
canonical shift is ergodic ([[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]), then
the limit is the constant $\mathbb EY_0$. For complex-valued processes the
assertions hold componentwise for real and imaginary parts.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

Assume AC. Let $(Z_{n,k},\mathcal F_{n,k})$ be a square-integrable martingale-difference array such that, for every $n$, $M_{n,m}$ and $\Gamma_{n,m}$ converge almost surely as $m\to\infty$ to finite limits $M_{n,\infty}$ and $\Gamma_{n,\infty}$. If
$$\Gamma_{n,\infty}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{in probability}$$
and, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$L_n(\varepsilon):=\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2 1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]\longrightarrow0,$$
then $M_{n,\infty}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
Let $1\le p<\infty$. If $X_n\to X$ in $L^p$, then $X_n\to X$ in probability.

Let $X_n$ and $Y_n$ be Borel-measurable random elements with values in a metric space $S$, on the same probability space for each $n$, and let $X$ be an $S$-valued Borel-measurable random element. Suppose $d(X_n,Y_n)$ is measurable and $P(d(X_n,Y_n)>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon$>0. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$, then $Y_n\Rightarrow X$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: For an integrable $Z$ and any integer $k$, the variable $\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_0]\circ T^k$ is $\mathcal F_k$ measurable because the pullback of $\mathcal F_0$ by $T^k$ is $\mathcal F_k$. Every event in $\mathcal F_k$ is the pullback of an event in $\mathcal F_0$, since $T$ is invertible and bimeasurable. Changing variables under the probability-preserving bijection $T^k$ proves that the integrals of this candidate and $Z\circ T^k$ agree over every $\mathcal F_k$ event. Uniqueness of conditional expectation therefore gives $\mathbb E[Z\circ T^k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_0]\circ T^k$ as almost-everywhere classes.

By summability and [F3], the partial sums defining $H_0$ are Cauchy in $L^2(\mathcal F_0)$ and have a limit there. Composition with $T^k$ is an $L^2$ isometry, so step 1.1 yields $H_k=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_k]$ in $L^2$, with $H_k$ measurable in $\mathcal F_k$ and $\|H_k\|_2=\|H_0\|_2$. Representatives may be fixed for the countably many indices; discard a countable union of null sets for their identities.

By [F1], conditional expectation is continuous in $L^2$. Apply [F2]'s tower property to the partial sums in step 1.2 and pass to the $L^2$ limit to obtain $\mathbb E[H_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb E[X_{k+j}\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=H_{k-1}-\mathbb E[X_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]$. Thus $D_k=X_k+H_k-H_{k-1}$ is square-integrable and $\mathcal F_k$ measurable, with $\mathbb E[D_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=0$. Also $D_k=D_1\circ T^{k-1}$, so the differences are stationary. Summing their defining identity gives $S_n=M_n+R_n$, where $M_n=\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$, $R_n=H_0-H_n$, and $\|R_n\|_2\le2\|H_0\|_2$. In particular $R_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability by [F8].

Put $q_0=\mathbb E[D_1^2\mid\mathcal F_0]$. It is nonnegative, integrable, and has expectation $\tau^2=\mathbb E[D_1^2]$ by [F1]. Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]=q_0\circ T^{k-1}$. The map $\omega\mapsto(q_0(T^j\omega))_{j\ge0}$ intertwines $T$ with the canonical one-sided shift. Hence a shift-invariant event for this process pulls back to a $T$-invariant event modulo null sets, whose probability is zero or one by the assumed ergodicity. The process is stationary, integrable and ergodic, so [F5] gives $n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb E[D_k^2\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\to\tau^2$ almost surely. The limiting variance is therefore a constant.

If $\tau^2>0$, let $Z_{n,k}=D_k/(\tau\sqrt n)$ for $1\le k\le n$, and let $Z_{n,k}=0$ for $k>n$; use the filtration $\mathcal F_{n,k}=\mathcal F_{\min(k,n)}$ for $k\ge0$. Step 1.3 makes each row a square-integrable martingale-difference row. The row sums and clocks are eventually constant, and step 2.1 shows their terminal clocks converge almost surely to $1$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, stationarity gives $\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|Z_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\}}]=\tau^{-2}\mathbb E[D_1^2\mathbf1_{\{|D_1|>\varepsilon\tau\sqrt n\}}]\to0$ by [F7]. Thus [F6] gives $M_n/(\tau\sqrt n)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. Scaling and the perturbation in step 1.3 give $S_n/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2)$ by [F8].

If $\tau^2=0$, stationarity implies $\mathbb E[D_k^2]=0$ for every $k$, so $M_n=0$ almost surely. Step 1.3 gives $S_n/\sqrt n\to0$ in $L^2$ and hence in probability. The constant sequence $0$ has weak limit the point mass $N(0,0)$; [F8] transfers that limit to $S_n/\sqrt n$. This establishes the asserted CLT in both variance cases.

Suppose the additional covariance summability holds, and put $\gamma_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_j)$. Stationarity and expansion of the finite square give $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)/n=\gamma_0+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-j/n)\gamma_j\to\gamma_0+2\sum_{j\ge1}\gamma_j$, by [F7] on counting measure with summable dominator $|\gamma_j|$. For $i<j$, $D_i$ is $\mathcal F_{j-1}$ measurable, so [F2], [F4], and step 1.3 give $\mathbb E[D_iD_j]=0$. Therefore $\mathbb E[M_n^2]=n\tau^2$. The identity $S_n=M_n+R_n$ and [F4] imply $|\mathbb E[S_n^2]-n\tau^2|/n\le\|R_n\|_2^2/n+2\|R_n\|_2\tau/\sqrt n\to0$, since $\|R_n\|_2$ is bounded. All $S_n$ are centered, so [F9] identifies the two variance limits and proves the stated covariance formula, including $\tau^2=0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume AC. For every positive integer $r$ there is a finite constant $C_r$, depending only on $r$, such that for every integer $n\ge1$, independent standard-normal variables $U_1,\ldots,U_n$, and real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix $A$,
$$E\left|U^TAU-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^{2r}\le C_r\left(\sum_{i,k=1}^n A_{ik}^2\right)^r.$$
In particular $E(U^TAU)=\operatorname{tr}A$. The matrix may be singular or indefinite.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\overline\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. Then for
every $x>0$
$$\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{1+x^2}\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x},$$
and consequently, for every $x>1$,
$$\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x}.$$
Both bounds are sharp as $x\to\infty$ in the sense that the ratio of each side
to $\overline\Phi(x)$ tends to $1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $V$ be a normed space. For all $x,y\in V$,
$$\bigl|\|x\|-\|y\|\bigr|\le \|x-y\|.$$
In particular, the norm map is $1$-Lipschitz for the norm metric.

**Inputs:** Real outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, an integer $n\ge2$, and an integer batch size $b$ with $1\le b<n$. For an MCMC run, $y_i=f(X_i)$ for the chosen real-valued observable $f$.

**Outputs:** The sample mean $\bar y_n$, the overlapping-batch-means estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}$, and its estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

1. Compute the sample mean
$$\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.$$

2. For each starting index $j=1,\ldots,n-b+1$, compute the overlapping batch mean
$$\bar y_j(b)=\frac1b\sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}y_i.$$

3. Return the overlapping-batch-means variance estimate
$$\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}=\frac{nb}{(n-b)(n-b+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b+1}\bigl(\bar y_j(b)-\bar y_n\bigr)^2.$$

4. Return the estimated Monte Carlo standard error
$$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar y_n)=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}/n}.$$

All sums are finite, the denominator is positive because $b<n$, and the variance estimate is nonnegative. The procedure always returns a number for the stated finite input. It does not by itself assert a CLT or consistency; consistency requires the hypotheses of the overlapping-batch-means theorem.

derivations.claim: Work first on the extension. For each sufficiently large $n$ write $b=b_n$, $m=n-b+1$, $U_i=B(i)-B(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le n$, and $D_j=B(j+b)-B(j)$ for $0\le j\le n-b$. By [F1], the $U_i$ are independent standard normals. If $h_j$ indicates coordinates $j+1,\ldots,j+b$, then $Q_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_jD_j^2=U^TA_nU$ where $A_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_jh_jh_j^T$. At most $b$ windows contain a fixed pair of coordinates, and none does if their separation is at least $b$. Hence $0\le(A_n)_{ik}\le1/n$, $(A_n)_{ik}=0$ when $|i-k|\ge b$, $\operatorname{tr}A_n=m/n$, and $\sum_{i,k}(A_n)_{ik}^2\le(2b-1)/n\le2b/n$.

Choose an integer $r\ge c$. By [F2] and [F3], for every $\eta>0$, $\Pr(|Q_n-m/n|>\eta)\le C_r\eta^{-2r}(2b_n/n)^r$. These probabilities are summable since $b_n/n<1$ eventually, $r\ge c$ and $\sum_n(b_n/n)^c<\infty$. Applying [F4] for each $\eta=1,1/2,1/3,\ldots$ and intersecting the resulting countable family of full-probability events gives $Q_n-m/n\to0$ almost surely. Since $m/n\to1$, $Q_n\to1$ almost surely. No independence between different $n$ is used.

By [F1] and [F5], $\Pr(|B(n)|>\sqrt{6n\log n})\le2n^{-3}$ for $n\ge2$. Thus [F4] gives $B(n)^2/n\le6\log n$ eventually almost surely. Put $V_j=D_j-(b/n)B(n)$ and $W_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_jV_j^2$. Applying [F6] to the vectors $(V_j)/\sqrt{nb}$ and $(D_j)/\sqrt{nb}$ gives $|\sqrt{W_n}-\sqrt{Q_n}|\le[(m/n)(b/n)(B(n)^2/n)]^{1/2}\to0$, using $(b_n/n)\log n\to0$. Consequently $W_n\to1$ almost surely.

Set $R_k=S_k-\sigma B(k)$ and $R_0=0$. On the full event of the given approximation, enlarge its finite random constant to absorb all finitely many early errors. Since $k^\alpha\log k$ is increasing for integers $k\ge2$, this gives a finite random $K'$ with $\max_{0\le k\le n}|R_k|\le K'n^\alpha\log n$ for every sufficiently large $n$. For every window, $S_{j+b}-S_j-(b/n)S_n=\sigma V_j+E_{n,j}$ where $E_{n,j}=R_{j+b}-R_j-(b/n)R_n$. Therefore $|E_{n,j}|\le3K'n^\alpha\log n$ simultaneously for all windows, and $H_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_jE_{n,j}^2\le9(K')^2(m/n)n^{2\alpha}(\log n)^2/b_n\to0$.

Put $T_n=(nb)^{-1}\sum_j(S_{j+b}-S_j-(b/n)S_n)^2$. By [F6] and $\sigma\ge0$, $|\sqrt{T_n}-\sigma\sqrt{W_n}|\le\sqrt{H_n}\to0$. Hence $T_n\to\sigma^2$ almost surely. This argument divides neither by $\sigma$ nor by $T_n$, so it also proves the zero-variance case.

By [F7], $\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{OBM},n}^2=n^2T_n/[(n-b_n)(n-b_n+1)]$. This deterministic multiplier tends to one because $b_n/n\to0$, and step 3.2 proves the desired limit on the extension. The event that this sequence of finite measurable functions of $(Y_i)$ converges to $\sigma^2$ depends only on the original process. Its probability under the extension equals its probability under the original marginal, so that probability is one for the original process as well. Arbitrarily defining the estimator at any finitely many indices with inadmissible batches does not affect its limit.
